title: Remove the tells that make a script sound machine-written
when: Drafting, reviewing or polishing a narration script, title or description.
summary: Machine-written scripts share recognisable habits: the same filler words, hedges in every sentence, dashes everywhere, every paragraph built the same way, vague claims and a closing paragraph that repeats the opening. Viewers hear them as 'AI voice' and stop trusting the channel.
do: Replace filler words such as delve, landscape, crucial, vital, pivotal, leverage, furthermore, moreover, navigate, robust, comprehensive, foster and facilitate with plain words, or cut them.
Keep hedges ('it is important to note', 'one might argue') to where uncertainty is real.
End by adding something new or landing the payoff, never by summarising what was just said.
avoid: A dash in every other sentence.
Every paragraph shaped claim, explanation, example, bridge.
checks: No more than one filler word from the list per minute of script.
The last paragraph does not restate the first.
source: alirezarezvani/claude-skills content-humanizer (MIT), pinned 8f08254: AI tell categories; restated for narration.

title: Vary sentence length so the ear stays awake
when: Writing or polishing narration, and directing how it is read.
summary: Uniform sentences of 18-22 words make the ear go numb. Narration needs deliberate variation: a long sentence that unwinds a thought, then a short one. A fragment for emphasis. A question, then its answer.
do: After a long sentence, put a short one.
Use a fragment where emphasis needs air.
Use patterns such as 'question, answer, proof' and 'claim, example, so what'.
avoid: Three sentences in a row of nearly the same length.
checks: Sentence lengths in each paragraph differ clearly.
source: alirezarezvani/claude-skills content-humanizer (MIT), pinned 8f08254: sentence rhythm; restated for spoken scripts.

title: Replace every vague claim with a specific one or an honest qualifier
when: Any claim in a script: amounts, studies, groups of people, results.
summary: Vague claims ('many companies', 'studies show', 'a lot of', 'significantly') invite doubt. Name the thing, give the number, cite the source from the evidence, or say plainly that it is a pattern rather than a measured fact.
do: Turn 'many' into a number or a named example from the evidence.
Turn 'studies show' into the named source, or drop the claim.
When no data exists, say so honestly instead of inventing authority.
avoid: Inventing a figure or a source to sound specific.
checks: Every claim of size or result names a number, a named example or an honest qualifier.
source: alirezarezvani/claude-skills content-humanizer and copywriting (MIT), pinned 8f08254; restated.

title: Long-form architecture: hook, context, body beats, one action
summary: Most viewers decide to stay in the first 30 seconds. After the hook, a short context says why it matters and who it is for; the body is a series of beats, each problem, solution, example, result; one clear action comes in the last minute.
steps: Hook (0-30 s): a problem, a counter-intuitive claim or a result promise.
Context (30-90 s): why this matters and what the viewer gets.
Body: one beat per point, each problem, solution, example, result; chapters for videos over 8 minutes.
Action (last 60 s): one clear next step.
avoid: A long introduction before the first beat.
checks: The first beat starts within 90 seconds.
There is one call to action, near the end.

title: Short-form: stop the scroll, one idea, one action
when: Writing a Short of 60 seconds or less.
summary: A Short has room for one idea. The first 3 seconds interrupt the scroll with a picture or statement; by 15 seconds the promise is clear; the value fills the middle; the last seconds give one action.
steps: 0-3 s: a pattern interrupt, before any title card.
3-15 s: the problem or promise.
15-50 s: the value.
50-60 s: one action.
avoid: Packing two ideas into one Short.
checks: The hook is on the first frame.

title: One target keyword, placed in four places
when: Packaging a video and writing its opening.
summary: Search is a large part of YouTube discovery. Pick one primary keyword per video and put it in the title (within the first 60 characters), in the first two sentences of the description, in the tags, and spoken in the first 30 seconds.
do: Choose one primary keyword from the topic's search language.
Place it in the title's first 60 characters.
Say it naturally in the first 30 seconds of narration.
avoid: Keyword stuffing that makes the title read badly.
checks: The keyword appears in the title, description opening and first 30 seconds.

title: A niche you can describe in one sentence
when: Evaluating or defining a channel's niche.
summary: A channel about a broad subject competes with every channel on it. A niche you can own is specific enough to describe the ideal viewer in one sentence: who they are, what problem they have, the channel's point of view and why it is credible.
steps: Write who the viewer is.
Write the problem they have.
Write the channel's distinct point of view.
Write why the channel is believable on it.
If the ideal viewer does not fit in one sentence, narrow the niche.
checks: The niche's ideal viewer is one sentence.

title: Three or four content pillars every video maps to
when: Planning a channel's topics or proposing new video ideas.
summary: Recurring topic categories make a channel predictable for subscribers and readable for recommendation. Typical pillars: how-to (search), comparisons (decision), case studies (trust), opinion (shareable).
do: Name 3-4 pillars for the channel.
Tag every proposed idea with its pillar.
Balance the pillars over a month of uploads.
checks: Every idea belongs to a named pillar.

title: Turn one long video into several Shorts
when: A long video is finished and the channel also publishes Shorts.
summary: One long piece holds several self-contained moments. Each one that makes a single point with its own hook can become a Short, re-framed vertically, captioned, and titled for its own search.
steps: Find 3-5 moments that make one point each and can stand alone.
Give each its own first-frame hook.
Re-frame for 9:16 and caption it.
Title each Short for its own keyword.
avoid: Cutting a moment that needs the rest of the video to make sense.

title: Benefits in the viewer's own words, one idea per section
when: Writing titles, thumbnail words, descriptions and calls to action.
summary: Clear beats clever. Say what the viewer gets, in the words viewers use themselves, specifically, one idea at a time.
do: Choose clarity over a clever pun.
Say the benefit, not the feature.
Use the words the audience uses in comments and searches.
Keep one idea per title or section.
avoid: Company or insider vocabulary the viewer does not use.
checks: A title says what the viewer gets in plain words.

title: Use the attention models that fit: curiosity gap, loss aversion, social proof, specificity
when: Writing hooks, titles and thumbnail words.
summary: A few well-known mental models explain why people click and stay: an open question the brain wants closed, the fear of losing something they have, evidence that others already care, and a specific number that sounds real. Use the one that is true for the video.
do: Open a curiosity gap the video really closes.
Frame stakes as what the viewer could lose when that is honest.
Use a specific number from the script instead of a round one.
avoid: A gap the video never closes (it reads as clickbait and hurts retention).
checks: The question opened by the hook is answered in the video.
source: alirezarezvani/claude-skills marketing-psychology (MIT), pinned 8f08254: most-used mental models; restated for YouTube.

title: Brief first, outline second, then write section by section
when: Starting a script from research or competitor examples.
summary: Good scripts start from a brief: what competitors already cover, the gap this video fills, the sources, the promise. Then an outline in beats, then each section written against its beat.
steps: Note what existing videos on the topic cover and miss.
Write the promise and the gap this video fills.
Outline the beats before writing prose.
Write each section against its beat and cut what does not serve it.
